conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes that the evidence is conflicting and mixed, detailing both trials/meta-analyses showing no benefit and others showing modest symptom improvement without taking a definitive stance.
conclusion.label: hedged

report:
The evidence on this question is actually mixed, not a clear "yes."

Multiple well-designed randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials have found **no benefit** from CoQ10 for statin-associated muscle symptoms. A rigorous crossover RCT designed specifically to confirm statin myalgia found that CoQ10 supplementation "had no effect on the incidence and severity of myalgia, time to onset of pain, muscle strength, or aerobic performance," despite successfully raising serum CoQ10 levels (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4298455/). Consistent with this, a widely cited meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials published in *Mayo Clinic Proceedings* (2015) concluded that CoQ10 has no significant effect on statin-induced myopathy, and clinical summaries built on this evidence recommend against using CoQ10 for this purpose, instead advising clinicians to investigate other causes of muscle symptoms (https://nerdcat.org/studysummaries/coq10-statin-myalgia).

However, not all evidence points the same way. A newer meta-analysis found that CoQ10 supplementation (50 mg twice daily) was associated with improvement in statin-associated muscle symptoms, including lower pain scores and reduced creatine kinase levels (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12536858/). Other sources cite a 2018 *Journal of the American Heart Association* meta-analysis reporting that CoQ10 "ameliorated" muscle symptoms like pain, weakness, and cramps, though this trial itself wasn't directly retrieved here—only secondary summaries referencing it.

**Bottom line:** The evidence is conflicting. Some rigorous individual RCTs and an influential 2015 meta-analysis found no benefit, while other, more recent meta-analyses report modest symptom improvement. Given this inconsistency, "yes" is an oversimplification—CoQ10 may help some patients, but the highest-quality individual trial evidence does not strongly support it, and conclusions depend heavily on which meta-analysis is consulted.
